glance: 200 km to Khulna by road, 5–7 hours by bus or car
pc-roy-birthplace-raruli.desc: Acharya Prafulla Chandra Ray, the chemist and founder of Bengal Chemicals, was born in this house at Raruli village in Paikgachha upazila on 2 August 1861. The house stands on the bank of the Kapotaksha river. After it was abandoned it was occupied several times, until the Department of Archaeology declared it a protected monument. Today it is a quiet stop with the old family buildings, and events are held here on his birth and death anniversaries.
blocks: How to get there
Bus from Khulna to Paikgachha, then a CNG, easy-bike or van to Raruli village.
Good to know
Ask locals for 'PC Roy-er bari'. Combine it with a trip along the Kapotaksha or to the shrimp country around Paikgachha.

glance: Indromohon Sweets, Helatola Road near Kalibari ghat, Khulna city
indromohon-sweets-khulna.desc: Indromohon is the sweet shop most Khulna people name first. It has been selling for well over a century, about 135 years by one count, from Helatola Road near the Kalibari ghat in the old part of the city. Its soft rosogolla and sandesh are the classics, and its mishti doi is still set in earthenware pots.
blocks: Good to know
Combine it with a walk around the Kalibari and the riverside.

glance: 200 km to Khulna by road, 5–7 hours by bus or car
kalabogi-stilt-village.desc: After Cyclone Aila flooded its fields in 2009, Kalabogi in Dacope rebuilt itself on bamboo poles over the tidal mud of the Shibsa river. Families now live in raised homes facing the Sundarbans across the water, storing rainwater in drums and earning from fishing and the forest. It is a working village rather than an attraction. A respectful visit shows the human side of the coast's climate story.
blocks: How to get there
Travel from Khulna to Dacope by road, then onward by local boat or bike towards Sutarkhali and Kalabogi.
Good to know
Ask before photographing people and homes; go with a local guide or NGO contact if you can.

glance: 200 km to Khulna by road, 5–7 hours by bus or car
Forest Department permit and fees apply; usually bundled into tour packages
khulna-sundarbans-cruise.desc: Most multi-day Sundarbans tours set off from the ghats of Khulna city, sailing down the Rupsha and Pasur rivers into the largest mangrove forest on earth. Boats sleep on board and use smaller dinghies to reach forest stations, walking trails and creeks where spotted deer, monkeys, crocodiles and many birds are seen. The Bengal tiger lives here but is rarely spotted. The journey itself, past fishing villages and shrimp ghers, is half the experience.
blocks: How to get there
Reach Khulna by train, bus or air via Jashore, then join a licensed tour boat from the city ghats.
Good to know

Entry needs a Bangladesh Forest Department permit and an armed forest guard, so book with a licensed operator who arranges both. Carry your passport or NID. Never walk off the marked trails, swim in the rivers or leave the group: tigers and crocodiles are real. Trips run mainly Nov–Mar; avoid the cyclone months and check weather warnings before departure.

glance: 200 km to Khulna by road, 5–7 hours by bus or car
winter (Dec–Jan), spring (Feb–Mar), summer (Apr–May), monsoon (Jun–Jul), autumn (Aug–Sep) and late autumn (Oct–Nov)
khulna-divisional-museum.desc: Opened in 1998 beside the Shib Bari crossing in the city centre, the divisional museum is run under the National Museum and the Department of Archaeology. By floor area it is the second-largest museum in the country. Its galleries hold terracotta plaques, stone sculptures, coins and household objects from excavations at Barobazar, Bharat Bhayna and Khan Jahan Ali's Bagerhat, along with photographs of the old monuments of greater Khulna. It is a good first stop before heading out to the sites themselves.
blocks: How to get there
It stands next to Zia Public Hall at Shib Bari more in central Khulna; any rickshaw or easy bike will take you there.
Good to know
Closed on Sundays (and half of Monday), so check the day before you go. Pair it with the Bagerhat mosques the same week; the objects make more sense afterwards.

glance: Varies by size, roughly 800–1,400 BDT per kg
Fish markets and local restaurants in Khulna city
golda-chingri.desc: Golda, the giant freshwater prawn, is farmed in the gher ponds around Khulna and sent all over the country. Large heads full of rich fat are part of the pleasure. Home cooks make malaikari with coconut milk, or a spicy bhuna with onions. Buying from a fish market and having a hotel cook it is a common local habit.

glance: 200 km to Khulna by road, 5–7 hours by bus or car
winter (Dec–Jan), spring (Feb–Mar), summer (Apr–May), monsoon (Jun–Jul), autumn (Aug–Sep) and late autumn (Oct–Nov)
gollamari-memorial.desc: During the Liberation War, people seized by the Pakistani army were held and tortured at the old radio station at Gollamari, then killed and thrown into the Gollamari canal. After Khulna was freed, around five truckloads of skulls and bones were recovered from the canal and its banks. A memorial now stands by the canal, about two kilometres from the city centre and next to the Khulna University campus. It is a quiet, sobering place to stop and remember.
blocks: How to get there
Take a rickshaw or easy bike from the city centre to Gollamari on the Khulna University road (15–20 minutes).
Good to know
Dress modestly and keep your voice low; this is a place of mourning. Combine it with a walk around the university campus next door.

glance: Hotels at Chuknagar bazar, Dumuria, and many restaurants in Khulna city
chuknagar-chui-jhal.desc: Chui is the stem of a climbing pepper plant grown across greater Khulna and Jashore. Cut into pieces and slow-cooked with mutton or beef, it gives a sharp, aromatic heat unlike chilli, and the softened chui itself is chewed for its flavour. Roadside hotels at Chuknagar on the Khulna–Satkhira road built a reputation on this dish. It is eaten with plain rice, often for lunch.

glance: 200 km to Khulna by road, 5–7 hours by bus or car
dakshindihi-rabindra-complex.desc: Dakshindihi village in Phultala is linked to the Tagore family: Mrinalini Devi, the poet's wife, came from here, and the house associated with her family has been restored as a memorial. The two-storey building holds photographs and a small display on Tagore's ties to the region. Around it are village ponds, fields and a bust of the poet. It makes a calm half-day outing from Khulna city.
blocks: How to get there
Take a bus or auto north from Khulna towards Phultala, then a rickshaw or easy bike to Dakshindihi.
Good to know
Opening hours can change; check locally and combine with lunch on the Jashore road.

glance: 200 km to Khulna by road, 5–7 hours by bus or car
bhutiar-padma-bil.desc: Bhutiar Bil is a large seasonal wetland in Terokhada, spreading partly into neighbouring Narail. In the wet months a stretch of it fills with sacred lotus, pink and white flowers standing above broad leaves. Local boatmen paddle small boats between the blooms. The flowers are freshest just after sunrise and begin to close as the day heats up.
blocks: How to get there
Go by bus or auto from Khulna to Terokhada, then a local vehicle to the bil edge and hire a small boat.
Good to know
Arrive between 7 and 8:30 am; the boats are small, so travel light and keep phones in a dry bag.

glance: 200 km to Khulna by road, 5–7 hours by bus or car
masjidkur-mosque.desc: Masjidkur sits in Koyra upazila, close to the Kapotaksha river and the Sundarbans. The mosque lay buried under forest and soil until it was uncovered after 1947, which is how it got its name, the mosque that was dug out. Archaeologists link it to followers of Khan Jahan Ali in the late 1400s. Nine domes in three rows rest on thick walls and four stone pillars, and traces of terracotta rosettes and floral scrolls survive around the mihrabs. Few travellers make it this far south, so you will likely have it to yourself.
blocks: How to get there
Take a bus from Khulna to Koyra via Paikgachha (a long half-day ride), then a motorbike or easy bike to Masjidkur; locals all know it.
Good to know
It is still a working mosque, so visit outside prayer times and dress modestly. Roads in Koyra can be poor after heavy rain; winter is easiest.

glance: Stalls at Rupsha ghat (around ghat no. 7), Khulna city, in the evening
rupsha-ghat-street-food.desc: In the evening, the ghats along the Rupsha in Khulna fill with people watching the boats and the bridge lights, and small stalls set up beside them. The fare is simple and cheap: ghugni, boiled potatoes, whole roasted garlic, mutton chop patties and endless cups of tea. Ghat number seven is the best-known spot. It is the easiest way to eat like a Khulna local.
blocks: Good to know
Go just before sunset and sit by the river.

glance: 200 km to Khulna by road, 5–7 hours by bus or car
rupsha-riverfront.desc: The Rupsha is Khulna's working river, busy with ferries, coasters, wooden cargo boats and fishermen. The long Khan Jahan Ali Bridge, often just called Rupsha Bridge, spans it south of the city and is a popular evening spot for locals. From the riverbanks you see the life of a port town in motion. A short boat crossing at the old Rupsha ghat is an easy way to get onto the water.
blocks: How to get there
A rickshaw or auto from central Khulna to Rupsha ghat or the bridge approach takes 15–30 minutes.
Good to know
Go in the late afternoon for softer light and cooler air.

glance: Trusted sellers in Khulna city and Koyra
sundarbans-honey.desc: Every spring, when mangrove trees such as khalisha and goran flower, collectors enter the Sundarbans under Forest Department passes to gather wild honey. The early khalisha honey is light and prized. Honey from the forest is sold in Khulna and the edge villages of Koyra and Dacope. Buy from trusted sellers, as mixed or adulterated honey is common.

moual-honey-hunters.desc: Mouals are traditional honey collectors from villages such as those in Koyra on the forest edge. Each season they set out in boats with a pass from the Forest Department, travelling in groups and smoking bees from hives high in the mangroves. Before entering the forest many offer prayers to Bonbibi, the forest guardian honoured by both Hindus and Muslims. The work is dangerous, and tiger attacks are part of local memory.
blocks: Good to know
Some tour operators can arrange meetings with honey-collecting families outside the season.
